blocks.md: **A panel follows the same people, firms or countries over time, which lets a regression compare each unit with itself. Panels differ in shape (many units over a few years, or a few units over many years) and in completeness: in micro surveys people miss interviews, leaving an unbalanced panel. The shape decides which of the methods in the next lectures is practical.**

blocks.title: Source
blocks.md: Sections 1 and 2 of `Regression_Lecture5.ipynb` (Panel Data Models) and section 1 of its mathematical appendix. The notebook becomes eight lectures, one per major heading (the two short opening sections are combined here): this one, [Econ 430 L24 The Pooled Panel Model](note:econ-430-l24-the-pooled-panel-model), [Econ 430 L25 The Fixed Effects Model](note:econ-430-l25-the-fixed-effects-model), [Econ 430 L26 The Random Effects Model](note:econ-430-l26-the-random-effects-model), [Econ 430 L27 Comparing Fixed and Random Effects](note:econ-430-l27-comparing-fixed-and-random-effects), [Econ 430 L28 Pooled, Fixed and Random Effects in Practice](note:econ-430-l28-pooled-fixed-and-random-effects-in-practice), [Econ 430 L29 The Hausman-Taylor Estimator](note:econ-430-l29-the-hausman-taylor-estimator) and [Econ 430 L30 Sets of Regression Equations](note:econ-430-l30-sets-of-regression-equations). The notebook recommends the `linearmodels` panel examples as a further resource.

A panel consists of a group of cross-sectional units (people, households, firms, states, countries) observed over time ([Panel Data](note:panel-data)). Write $N$ for the number of units and $T$ for the number of periods; an observation is $(y_{it}, x_{it})$. Panels come in three shapes:

| Shape | $N$ and $T$ | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Long and narrow | Long time dimension, few units | Two firms' investment over 20 years |
| Short and wide | Many units, few periods | 716 women interviewed 5 times |
| Long and wide | Both large | Many countries over many decades |

Data can combine cross sections and time without being a panel: a survey that samples a fresh set of people each year is a set of **repeated cross sections**, because the individuals are not the same in each period.

blocks.prompt: A labour survey interviews a new random sample of 5,000 adults every year for ten years. Is this a panel?

options.md: Yes, a short and wide panel with $N = 5{,}000$ and $T = 10$
options.feedback: A panel needs the *same* units in each period; here each year's people are different.

options.md: No: it is a set of repeated cross sections, since no person is observed twice
Yes, a long and narrow panel
options.feedback: The shape labels apply only to panels, and this is not one.
Balance is a property of panels; this data set does not follow individuals at all.

blocks.why: The defining feature of a panel is repeated observation of the same unit, which is what lets a model compare each unit with itself. Repeated cross sections can track averages over time but not individuals.

blocks.md: In microeconomic panels individuals are not always interviewed the same number of times, which gives an **unbalanced panel**, with different numbers of time-series observations across individuals. In a **balanced panel** each individual has the same number of observations, $NT$ in total. The wage panel used in the following lectures is balanced: 716 women, each observed in 1982, 1983, 1985, 1987 and 1988, for 3,580 observations.

blocks.prompt: A firm panel has 200 firms; 150 are observed in all 8 years and 50 in only 6. How many observations are there?

wrong.md: that uses 6 years for every firm

blocks.why: $150 \times 8 + 50 \times 6 = 1{,}200 + 300 = 1{,}500$. The panel is unbalanced, so the total is not $N \times T$.
